issues.legal_issue: The State may not lease ecologically fragile natural resources held in public trust for private commercial use without lawful authority consistent with the trust.
material_facts: The State leased protected forest land beside a river to a commercial motel, including additional land situated on the river’s flood plain between its main channel and a natural spill channel.
The motel had encroached on part of the additional land before it was leased and used the land for its commercial resort.
The Government of India granted prior approval under Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and the State then executed the additional lease.
The court found that the land was ecologically fragile and that the lease was for private commercial purposes, not a demonstrated public necessity.
issues.conclusion: The State breached its public-trust duty by granting the additional lease. The prior approval and lease were quashed, the lease was cancelled, and the State was directed to take over the land and restore it to its natural condition. The river bank and basin were to remain open for public use, and the motel was not to encroach on or use the river basin.
issues.legal_principle: The public trust doctrine is part of Indian law. The State holds natural resources, including running waters, forests and ecologically fragile lands, as trustee for public use and enjoyment and has a legal duty to protect them. In the absence of legislation authorizing the relevant action, the executive cannot surrender those resources to private ownership or commercial use; departure from the trust is permissible only when justified in good faith by the public interest. The Court relied on the reasoning in Illinois Central Railroad Co. v. Illinois, Gould v. Greylock Reservation Commission, Sacco v. Department of Public Works, Robbins v. Department of Public Works, National Audubon Society v. Superior Court (the Mono Lake case), and Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Mississippi. It applied that doctrine to the approval and lease made under Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_proceeding and state_controls_natural_resource and ecologically_fragile_public_resource and state_grants_private_commercial_use and not public_interest_necessity and not legislative_authorization

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The matter was brought as a public-interest proceeding concerning environmental protection.
predicates.state_controls_natural_resource: The State held or controlled a natural resource for the benefit of the public.
predicates.ecologically_fragile_public_resource: The resource was ecologically fragile and part of the natural environment.
predicates.state_grants_private_commercial_use: The State granted the resource for private commercial use.
predicates.public_interest_necessity: The grant was necessary in good faith to serve the public interest.
predicates.legislative_authorization: Legislation authorized the State to make the grant consistently with its public-trust duty.

issues.definition: When the State controls an ecologically fragile public resource and grants it for private commercial use without legislative authorization or a public-interest necessity, the additional lease must be set aside and the land restored.

issues.legal_issue: An actor whose unauthorized interference with a natural watercourse causes environmental damage must bear the cost of restoring the damaged environment.
material_facts: The motel constructed embankments and other works along the river and dredged and channelized its flow, including works that blocked the mouth of a natural spill channel.
The motel undertook the works without permission from the relevant department and without expert advice.
The court found that the motel’s constructions and interference with the river’s natural flow degraded the environment and ecology of the area.
The court directed the motel to pay compensation for environmental restitution and directed an expert assessment of the likely restoration cost.
issues.conclusion: The motel was directed to pay the cost of restitution of the environment and ecology damaged by its works, with the amount to be assessed. It was also directed to show cause why an additional pollution fine should not be imposed.
issues.legal_principle: The polluter-pays principle means that liability for environmental harm includes both compensation to affected persons and the cost of restoring the damaged environment. A person carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is liable for harm caused by that activity irrespective of whether reasonable care was taken. The Court relied on Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, which recognized the precautionary and polluter-pays principles as essential features of sustainable development and part of Indian law, and Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, which applied the polluter-pays principle and absolute liability.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The matter was brought as a public-interest proceeding concerning environmental protection.
predicates.actor_interferes_with_natural_watercours: An actor carried out works that interfered with a natural watercourse without authorization.
predicates.actor_causes_environmental_damage: The actor’s works caused damage to the environment or ecology.

issues.definition: When an actor interferes with a natural watercourse without authorization and causes environmental damage in an environmental public-interest proceeding, the actor must pay the cost of restoring the environment.
